finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> performs no authorization. The return value of is_allowed() is discarded, so any caller can delete any stored file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client that can reach DELETE /files/<fid>. No credential is needed; the caller only needs a fid that exists in STORE.
finding.sink: views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]`, a destructive write to a resource the caller is not authorized to modify.

trace.note: load_user sets g.user from the request header, which may be absent (None).
f = STORE[fid] loads the resource by URL id with no owner or tenant check.
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') is is_allowed imported under an alias. Its bool result is dropped, so it never aborts.
is_allowed returns False for g.user=None or a user without the 'delete' grant; the False is ignored at views.py:18.
The file is deleted regardless of the check result.

finding.guards_checked: before_request hook (views.py:10-12) only copies a header and does not reject. is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) is a correct predicate but has no enforcing effect here. No decorator or auth middleware present. rename_file (views.py:26) uses ensure_allowed, which aborts on denial, so the delete route is the defective one.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. views.py:10-12 (before_request) only copies a header and never rejects. views.py:18 calls require_allowed (alias of acl.py:4 is_allowed, a bool predicate) and discards the result; no decorator or middleware exists, and the directory holds only acl.py and views.py. The working guard ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts on denial) is used only by rename_file at views.py:26, not delete_file.
verdict.reason: At views.py:18 the bool returned by is_allowed (acl.py:5) is discarded as a bare statement, so the unconditional `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19 runs for any caller, including anonymous (g.user=None, which acl.py:5 evaluates to False), and the claimed trace is accurate on every line.

finding.claim: Caller identity comes from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification. A client that reaches the service directly can impersonate any user.
finding.source: Any HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified set to a target username. Precondition: the service is reachable without a trusted reverse proxy that strips and rewrites this header.
finding.sink: g.user, used by every authorization check (views.py:18 and views.py:26 via acl.py:5 grants.get(user)).

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') with no signature, session, or origin check.
grants.get(user, []) uses the value as the lookup key, so a forged name selects that user's grants.
rename_file's ensure_allowed passes for any user name the attacker sends.

finding.guards_checked: No upstream middleware or proxy config is in the repo to show the header is stripped or set. If the deployment guarantees the header is overwritten at the edge, this is not exploitable and should be dropped. Severity depends on that deployment fact, which could not be verified from this code.

verdict.guard_found: None in the repo. views.py:12 takes the header unchecked. acl.py:5 is a plain dict lookup keyed on the header value. The only candidate guard is external: a reverse proxy that strips or overwrites X-Session-User-Verified, which is not in this repo.
verdict.reason: The lines cited are accurate: views.py:12 trusts the header with no check, acl.py:5 uses it as the grants key, and views.py:26 passes via abort(403) only when the grant exists. Whether an anonymous client can reach the app directly, which is the deciding fact, cannot be determined from this code. The trace is wrong at views.py:18, where require_allowed (is_allowed, a bool-returning function) is a bare statement whose result is discarded, so DELETE /files/<fid> has no authorization check at all; the candidate describes that line as an effective authorization check.
